parole.significato: A toponymic suffix indicating a castle, fortress, manor or estate.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -stein, from Middle High German stein (“stone”). Never used in this form outside of compounds in Dutch, this toponymic suffix started being adopted from Middle High German toponymy in the 13th century and has remained somewhat productive as a toponymic suffix in Dutch to the presen
From Middle Dutch aendachte, from Middle High German andaht, from Old High German anadāht. Cognate to German Andacht. Equivalent to aan (“on”) + dacht (“thought”).

From Middle Dutch ampt. Originally the same word as ambacht and possibly a mere variant of it. However, the fact that the earliest occurrences are found in texts by eastern writers, makes it likely that this form is a borrowing from Middle High German ambet, ambt (whence modern German Amt), from Old
From Middle Dutch arsenie, from Middle High German arzenie. Equivalent to arts + -enij. Compare German Arznei.
From Middle Dutch barmhertich, from Middle High German barmherzec, Old High German barmherzi, calque from Latin misericors. Equivalent to barmen (see erbarmen) + hart + -ig.
From Middle Dutch bryts (“lattice”), from Middle High German britze, from Old High German [Term?].
From Middle Dutch brullen, from Middle High German brüelen (modern brüllen), ultimately imitative.
From Middle Dutch degen, from Middle High German degen, itself borrowed from Old French dague (“dagger”).

From late Middle Dutch diefstal, from Middle High German diepstale, from diep (“thief”) + stale (“theft”). The former part has the same origin as dief, the latter is from Old High German stāla, from Proto-Germanic *stēlō. Replaced the Middle Dutch word diefte, which still survives in some dialects.
From Middle Dutch ervaren, from Middle High German ervarn. Equivalent to er- + varen (“to travel, to go”).
From Middle Dutch itlijc, from Middle High German etelich (German etliche).
From late Middle Dutch frisch, vrisch, borrowed from Middle High German vrisch, from Old High German frisc, from Proto-West Germanic *frisk, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz. Doublet of vers.
From Middle Dutch gansch, gans, gands, gants, borrowed from Middle High German ganz, from Old High German, from Proto-West Germanic *gant (“all, whole, entire”).
From Middle Dutch gasse (“unpaved street”), from Middle High German gazze, from Old High German gazza, from Proto-Germanic *gatwǭ.
From Middle Dutch gebrukelijc, from Middle High German gebrûchlich (whence German gebräuchlich). By surface analysis, gebruiken + -e- + -lijk.
From Middle Dutch gestalt, from Middle High German gestalt. Compare German Gestalt.
From Middle Dutch gestrenge, possibly borrowed from Middle High German gestrenge. By surface analysis, ge- + streng.
From Middle Dutch glans (ca. 1400), from Middle High German glanz (“shine, lustre”), whence Modern German Glanz.

parole.significato: to enforce, to maintain, to uphold
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hanthaven, from Middle High German hanthaben, itself a calque from Old French maintenir, from Vulgar Latin manūteneō. Likely based also on Middle Dutch handhave (“handle”). Cognate with German handhaben.
From Middle Dutch hars, harst, from Middle High German harz (modern German Harz), from Old High German harz, from Proto-West Germanic *hart, from Proto-Germanic *hartą.
From Middle Dutch hexe (15th c.), borrowed from Late Middle High German hecse. Displaced native Middle Dutch hagetisse. Both ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *hagatussjā.
From Middle Dutch hellebaert, hellebarde, from earlier helmbaerde, possibly from Middle High German helmbarte.
From Middle Dutch hitsich, from Middle High German hitzic, from hitze (“heat”). Doublet of hittig.
From Middle Dutch onger, honger. An earlier borrowing than Hongaar (which has stress on the second syllable), probably via Middle High German [Term?]. Unrelated to honger (“hunger”).
From Middle Dutch hutte, from Middle High German hütte, from Old High German hutta, from Proto-Germanic *hudjǭ.
From Middle Dutch inbegrepen, a calque from Middle High German.
Loaned from Middle High German inbrunst (“passion”), but reinterpreted as coming from in (“in”) + borst (“breast, chest”).

parole.significato: chancellor, high officer in a government, princely court, court of justice, order of chivalry, diplomatic or consular m…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch cancelier, canceler, from Middle High German kanzeler but influenced by Old French chancelier, both from Latin cancellārius.

parole.significato: Long cloth from the shoulders to the feet.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kuerse, probably borrowed via Middle High German kürsen (“fur garment”), from Old High German kursina (“fur”), from Old East Slavic кꙋрьзно (kurĭzno), from Proto-Slavic *kъrzьno (“fur coat”) (whence Russian корзно́ (korznó, “coat with fur trimming”)). Compare Middle Low German kors

parole.significato: Elector, Prince-Elector (of the Holy Roman Empire)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch coorvorst, likely from Middle High German [Term?]. Equivalent to keur + vorst.

Uncertain. Perhaps borrowed from Middle High German *knellen (as in Middle High German zerknellen (“to crumple, crush, shatter, squash”)), perhaps from Middle High German knellen (“to bang, burst”), whence archaic German knellen (“to bang, slam, pop”).

From Middle Dutch coorts, corts, curts. Related to Middle Low German korts (“fever”), possibly abbreviated from a phrase containing korts (“short”), from Middle High German kurz. An indirect relationship with kool (“coal”) has been suggested, via Proto-Indo-European *ǵwelH- (“burn, shine”); compare
From Middle Dutch craem, from Middle High German krām, from Old High German krām. Probably from a Slavic language, such as Old Church Slavonic грамъ (gramŭ, “pub, inn”) or чрѣмъ (črěmŭ, “tent”).
From Middle Dutch crans, from Middle High German kranz, from Old High German kranz, probably altered from krenz, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *kringaz (“circle, ring”).

parole.significato: to scratch on a hard, even surface
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch crassen, probably from Middle High German kratzen, from Old High German krazzōn, from Proto-Germanic *krattōną, presumably of imitative origin, but compare Albanian gërresë. Cognate with modern German kratzen, Middle Low German kratten. From a variant *kratjaną stem Middle Dutch cr

parole.significato: public peace, landfriede, constitutio pacis (internal peace imposed on a region or realm, esp. by subordinate forces or…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch lantvrēde, likely from Middle High German [Term?]. Equivalent to land + vrede.

From Middle Dutch lins, lynsen, from Middle High German linse, from Old High German linsa, likely a borrowing from an unidentified source. Compare Latin lēns, Lithuanian lęšis, and Old Church Slavonic лѧща (lęšta) sounding too similar for a coincidence, however different enough to prohibit reconstru
From Middle Dutch mangelen, from Middle High German mangeln.

parole.significato: compassion, sympathy for the suffering of another
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch medeliden, from Middle High German mitelīden (German Mitleid). Equivalent to mede (“with, along”) + lijden (“suffering”).
From Middle Dutch narre, borrowed from Middle High German narre, from Old High German narro, further etymology unknown; compare German Narr.
From Middle High German ūrochse, from Old High German ūrohso (compare German Auerochse).
From Middle High German ungevēr, ungevār (modern German ungefähr), a contraction of āne gevære (“without danger”).

From Middle Dutch panser, from Middle High German pantzer, from Old French panciere (whence Middle Dutch panchier), from panse (“belly”), from Medieval Latin panceria. The current spelling and pronunciation has been influenced by German Panzer.
From Middle High German praht, southern variety of braht, from Old High German braht, praht, from Proto-Germanic *brahtaz (“cracking, snapping, noise”). Related to breken (“to break, to snap”).
From Middle Dutch reisiger, borrowed from Middle High German reisiger (“soldier on horseback”), from reise (“war expedition”), cognate with Dutch reis (“travel”).

parole.significato: a rittmaster, a cavalry officer of a rank equivalent to captain
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ritmeester, from Middle High German [Term?]. Equivalent to rit + meester.
From Middle Dutch ritsen, from Middle High German ritzen, from Old High German rizzen, from Proto-West Germanic *rittjan, equivalent to rits (“zipper”) + -en. Cognate with English rit.
From Middle Dutch schertz, from Middle High German scherz, from or related to Old High German skeran (“to shave”), as in the second element of gekscheren (“to joke, make fun of”).
From Middle Dutch schertzen, from Middle High German scherzen. Equivalent to scherts + -en.
From Middle Dutch schranke, from Middle High German schranc. Related to German Schrank, English shrank (“cabinet”).
From Middle Dutch cieren, tsieren, sieren, borrowed from Middle High German zieren. Cognate with German zieren and the inherited form tieren.

parole.significato: to be sloppy, to be careless, to be slovenly
parole.testo: Possibly a frequentative (with expressive gemination) based on Middle High German *sloten (“to beat, tremble”), but that word appears late, infrequently, and as a back-formation. Perhaps instead related to a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as English

Likely borrowed from Middle High German sloger or Middle Low German sloier, of unknown ultimate origin. There is a possible connection to Latin stragulus (“covering”) and thus its borrowing Scottish Gaelic sròl (“satin”). Related to German Schleier, Danish slør, Swedish slöja.
From Middle Dutch spiesse, borrowed from Middle High German spiez, from Old High German spioz, from Proto-West Germanic *speut (“spear”). Cognate to spit and spiet.
Borrowed from Middle High German stengel, from Old High German stengil, from Proto-West Germanic *stangil, from Proto-Germanic *stangilaz. By surface analysis, stang + -el, with umlaut.
Inherited from Middle Dutch stifte, from Middle High German stift, from Old High German stift, from Proto-West Germanic *stift.

From Middle Dutch straffen, probably from Middle High German strāfen, which may go back to Proto-West Germanic *strēpōn, of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly related to *streupan (“to squeeze, press, graze”). The short vowel and geminate in Dutch in contrast to the Middle High German long vowe

parole.significato: an interpreter, one who translates/interprets speech in another language and vice versa
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch tolic, from Middle High German tolk, from Old East Slavic тълкъ (tŭlkŭ), толкъ (tolkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tъlkъ.

From Middle Dutch truerich, from Middle High German trūrec, from Old High German trūreg, trūrag, from Proto-Germanic *dreuzagaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrews- (“to break, break off, crumble”). Equivalent to treuren (“to grieve”) + -ig (“-y”). Cognate with Low German trurig, German traurig, Engli

First attested in 1515. Frequentative in -elen to an otherwise unattested verb *troeten which, given its initial t- (reflecting the High German consonant shift), is taken to be derived from Middle High German triuten. Ultimately a verbal formation based on Proto-Germanic *drūdaz (“dear, beloved”), a

From earlier vendel (the present form with -aa- is likely influenced by vaan), likely an earlier borrowing from Middle High German venel, diminutive (with umlaut) of vane (German Fahne). By surface analysis, vaan + -el, with epenthetic -d- (compare Dutch daalder).
From (rare) Middle Dutch vertwîvelen, most likely a calque of Middle High German verzwīveln (12th c., whence modern verzweifeln). By surface analysis, ver- + twijfelen (“to doubt”).
From Middle Dutch verwaerlosen, equivalent to obsolete waarloos (“careless, unmindful”) + ver- -en. Ultimately from Middle High German verwarlōsen, thereby a cognate with modern German verwahrlosen.
From Middle Dutch voltrecken (14th c.), probably after Middle High German volleziehen, from Old High German follaziohan (8th c.), whence German vollziehen. Equivalent to vol- + trekken.
From Middle Dutch voorneem, voornaem, from Middle High German vornēme.
From Middle Dutch wijnsteen, probably after Middle High German wīnstein, whence modern German Weinstein. By surface analysis, wijn (“wine”) + steen (“stone”).

Derived from Middle Dutch wyppen (first attested in 1477), from Middle High German wipfen (“to jump”), from Proto-Germanic *wipjan- (“to move up and down”), probably related to *waibijaną (“to move around”).

From Middle Dutch *samelen, reflected in the early 15th-century Middle Dutch samelinge. The word is generally considered to be borrowed from German; if this word indeed existed in Middle Dutch, then it would be borrowed from Middle High German samelen.

parole.significato: Third person singular and plural reflexive pronoun; himself, herself, itself, themselves, oneself
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sich, from Middle High German sich, from Old High German sih, from Proto-West Germanic *sik, from Proto-Germanic *sek. Old Dutch did not have a reflexive pronoun (only rarely in early Limburgish texts), but used the normal accusative pronoun (if necessary intensified by selven, cf.

From Middle Dutch sintvloed, from Middle High German sintvluot. The first element, which was originally the Germanic prefix *sin- (“everlasting, eternal”) (compare zenegroen), was folk-etymologically reinterpreted to yield a compound zonde (“sin”) + vloed (“flood”), as the biblical Deluge was the re
From Middle Dutch swetsen, from Middle High German swetzen, from swateren (“to clatter, rustle”), probably ultimately of imitative origin. Cognate with German schwätzen.
